Base directory for this skill: /Users/rodrigooliveira/git/roo-oliv/monodreams/.claude/skills/deep-review

# deep-review

Six parallel agents, each wearing one lens, review the change. Then a
consolidation pass dedupes, verifies, and classifies findings. The
output is a single structured review the user can post to GitHub,
copy, save, or discard.

Always quote file paths and line numbers in findings. Never paraphrase
code from memory — every Blocker/High finding must be re-verified by
reading the actual file.

---

## Phase 0 — Resolve the input

Parse the user's argument and determine review mode. Run input
parsing yourself; do not delegate to an agent.

**Argument shapes:**
- *(no argument)* — review the **current branch** vs `origin/main`,
  including uncommitted working-tree changes. Diff:
  `git diff origin/main...HEAD` plus `git diff` for uncommitted.
- *URL containing `/pull/<n>` or starts with `#<n>` or pure numeric* —
  **PR mode**. Extract the PR number; check it out with
  `gh pr checkout <n>`; diff with `gh pr diff <n>`.
- *7–40 hex characters* — **commit mode**. Check out with
  `git checkout <sha>`; diff with `git diff <sha>~1 <sha>`.
- *Anything else not matching above* — treat as a branch name; check
  out with `git checkout`; diff vs `origin/main`.

**Eco / fast mode.** If the user passes `--eco` or `--cheap` or
`--fast`, swap the deep-thinking agents (System-Ordering,
Cross-Domain, ECS-Purity) to Sonnet via the agent `model: sonnet`
override. Keep Adjacent-Code and Component-Design on Opus regardless
— they're the highest-value lenses.

**Abort conditions.** Stop with a clear error if:
- The checkout fails. Do not proceed against the wrong branch — the
  whole review becomes hallucinated. Surface the git error to the user.
- The diff is empty. Tell the user there's nothing to review.
- The working tree has uncommitted changes that would be clobbered by
  the checkout. Ask before stashing.

**Capture context for later phases:**
- The full diff (save to a temp file if large).
- The list of files changed (`git diff --name-only` against the right
  base).
- The mode (PR / branch / commit / local) for the output phase.

---

## Phase 1 — Gather framework context

Read these files yourself (don't delegate). Every agent in Phase 2
gets the **diff + the full text of each of these** in its prompt.

1. **`docs/CORE_TENETS.md`** — always.
2. **`docs/<domain>/premises.md`** for each domain whose files were
   touched. Domain detection:
   - `MonoDreams/Component/Draw/**`, `MonoDreams/System/Draw/**`,
     `MonoDreams/Renderer/**` → **rendering**.
   - `MonoDreams/Component/Collision/**`,
     `MonoDreams/System/Collision/**` → **collision**.
   - `MonoDreams/Component/Physics/**`,
     `MonoDreams/System/Physics/**` → **physics**.
   - `MonoDreams/Component/Transform.cs`, `Component/ChildOf.cs`,
     `Component/LayoutNode.cs`, `System/HierarchySystem.cs`,
     `System/TransformCommitSystem.cs`, `System/SizeSystem.cs`,
     `System/LayoutSystem.cs`, `State/EntityHierarchy.cs` →
     **hierarchy-transform**.
   - `MonoDreams/Component/Level/**`, `MonoDreams/System/Level/**`,
     `MonoDreams/System/EntitySpawn/**`, `MonoDreams/EntityFactory/**`,
     `MonoDreams/Message/EntitySpawnRequest.cs`,
     `MonoDreams/Message/Level/**` → **level-loading**.
   - If a path is in `MonoDreams.Examples/**`, include the
     foundational five premises files (they exercise everything).
3. **`.claude/CLAUDE.md`** — always.
4. **`MonoDreams.Examples/Screens/LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs`** —
   the reference pipeline assembly. Agents that check ordering need
   this verbatim.

If a touched file's domain isn't in the V1 premises set (Camera,
Cursor, Input, Debug, Screen, Messages/State), note "no premises file
exists for this domain (deferred to V2)" and proceed; the other
agents still apply.

---

## Phase 2 — Spawn six parallel review agents

Send all six in a single message, each with `Agent` tool, type
`general-purpose` (or the eco-mode override). Pass each the diff + the
gathered context + its persona + its checklist.

Every agent returns findings in this format:

```
**[Blocker | High | Medium | Low] — <one-line title>**
File: <path>:<line>
What: <what the change does>
Why it's a problem: <which tenet/premise/contract it violates>
Suggested fix: <concrete fix or "needs design discussion">
```

If an agent has nothing to report, it returns `No findings.` Don't
ask agents to invent findings.

### Agent 1 — Adjacent-Code (mandatory, Opus)

**Persona.** You are the engineer who knows every reference to every
public symbol in MonoDreams. When a method signature changes, you've
already opened every caller. When an enum gains a value, you've
already checked every switch statement and filter. You catch the
"forgot to update X downstream" class of bug that diff-only reviewers
always miss.

**Embedded tenets.** Read CORE_TENETS §2 and §7. The framework is a
network of components, systems, and messages with implicit
references; a diff shows only what changed, not what should have
changed in response.

**Checklist.**
1. Extract semantic changes from the diff:
   - New `enum` values (`DrawElementType`, `RenderTargetID`,
     `CollisionType`, status enums, etc.).
   - Changed method or constructor signatures on public types.
   - New fields on components.
   - New status / mode / type discriminators.
   - New factory identifiers registered.
   - New layers (`ActiveLayers`) or render targets.
2. For each semantic change, grep the entire repo for callers and
   pattern matches:
   - `grep -rn` on the symbol name across `MonoDreams/`,
     `MonoDreams.Examples/`, `MonoDreams.Tests/`,
     `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/`.
   - For enum values: grep the enum type and every `switch` /
     `case` / `==` / `.Where(... == ...)`.
3. Always grep these **engine anchors** even if the diff doesn't seem
   to touch them — they're the high-fan-out cores:
   - `MasterRenderSystem` — anywhere it switches on
     `DrawElementType`.
   - `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` — anywhere it dispatches by
     collider type.
   - `EntitySpawnSystem.RegisterFactory` — anywhere a factory is
     registered, and the dispatch site.
   - `HierarchySystem` — anywhere child / parent links are read.
   - `LevelLoadRequestSystem` — anywhere it adds
     `CurrentLevelComponent`.
   - `LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs` — the reference pipeline
     assembly.
4. For each grep hit, open the file and verify the code handles the
   new behavior. If not → finding.
5. **Inverse check.** Does the new code handle all *existing*
   scenarios it didn't before? A new filter that doesn't cover all
   pre-existing enum values is the same bug class as a missed caller.

### Agent 2 — System-Ordering / Pipeline (mandatory, Opus)

**Persona.** You are the engineer who has walked
`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` more times than anyone. You
think in pipeline phases: input → logic → physics (Movement →
Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit) → hierarchy → camera →
cull → prep → render. Ordering bugs are silent — the wrong order
doesn't throw, it just produces stale data.

**Embedded tenets.** CORE_TENETS §7 — the reference pipeline. The
ECS-purity rule: systems are pure functions; ordering is the screen's
responsibility. A system that quietly depends on another system
having run is a bug, and the assembler that orders them is the place
to catch it.

**Checklist.**
1. Identify any new system added by the diff, or any system whose
   registration order changed.
2. For each: determine where it lives in the reference pipeline
   shape. Use the per-frame phases as anchors:
   - Input
   - Game logic
   - Physics block (Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution →
     Commit)
   - Hierarchy / size / layout
   - Camera
   - Cursor
   - Render block (Culling → Sprite prep → YSort → Text prep → Mesh
     prep → Master render → Debug overlays)
3. Check the screen's registration site for the new/moved system.
   Confirm it lands in the correct phase.
4. **Execution-order check.** A new filter / query that runs before a
   transition or commit that hasn't fired yet returns empty. Read
   each Phase 2 system that filters by `Visible`, by `ColliderTag`,
   by `CurrentLevelComponent`, by `Velocity`, by `Transform.Delta`,
   etc., and verify the system that *produces* that filter is
   ordered before it.
5. If a touched system reads `Transform.WorldPosition` /
   `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`, verify `HierarchySystem` runs
   before it.
6. If a touched system reads `Transform.Delta`, verify
   `TransformCommitSystem` is at the tail of the previous frame
   (i.e., last in the pipeline before the new frame).
7. If a touched system writes `LayerDepth`, verify it runs **before**
   `MasterRenderSystem` and check whether it stomps on `YSortSystem`.

### Agent 3 — Component-Design / Framework-Fit (mandatory, Opus)

**Persona.** You are the engineer who hates the engine's primary
failure mode: hyper-specialized components that solve today's pain
but don't generalize. You ask "would this primitive be useful to a
feature 6 months from now under a different name?" before any new
component lands. You also know every existing component and can
spot when a PR re-invents one under a new name.

**Embedded tenets.** CORE_TENETS §1 (framework, not library) and §2
(ECS purity & composition). The single highest-value finding type
is: *added a super specialized component/system that solves one
specific pain point right now but doesn't evolve well in the framework
to deliver value for more implementations and play nice with other
features in MonoDreams.*

**Checklist.**
1. For each new component (any file added under
   `MonoDreams/Component/**` or `MonoDreams.Examples/Component/**`):
   1. Verify it is **pure data**. No methods beyond trivial property
      getters / setters. Any logic-shaped method → finding.
   2. Search for existing components that could be extended instead.
      Look at `Transform`, `DrawComponent`, `SpriteInfo`,
      `RigidBody`, `Velocity`, `BoxCollider`, `ConvexCollider`,
      `EntityInfo`, `CameraFollowTarget`, and the LayoutNode /
      ChildOf / Visible family. If the new component overlaps any of
      these conceptually, propose extending the existing one instead.
   3. Ask the framework-fit question: *would another feature reach
      for this primitive under a different name?* If yes, the
      naming/shape is game-shaped, not framework-shaped. Propose a
      generalization.
   4. Verify namespace placement. New components in
      `MonoDreams/Component/**` or
      `MonoDreams.Examples/Component/**`. **Never** put one under
      `MonoDreams.Entity` (shadows `DefaultEcs.Entity`).
2. For each new system, ask the same generalization question: is
   this a framework primitive, or did we hard-code today's feature?
3. If the diff adds a new draw/render component (anything that
   carries pixels or layer-depth besides `DrawComponent`,
   `SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`, `NinePatchInfo`): **Blocker**. The
   unification of rendering through `DrawComponent` is one of the
   most load-bearing tenets — see Rendering premises.

### Agent 4 — Cross-Domain Dependency (Opus, eco-swappable to Sonnet)

**Persona.** You are the engineer who keeps the premises files'
`Depends on:` graph in your head. You know that "swept collision
reads `Transform.Delta`" depends on "Delta is meaningful only after
`TransformCommitSystem` ran", and you flag any PR that touches one
side without considering the other.

**Embedded tenets.** Each domain's `premises.md` `Depends on:`
section. CORE_TENETS §2 — premises with `Depends on:` cross-refs
are how the framework's parts know they're connected.

**Checklist.**
1. List the domains touched by the diff (use the same routing as
   Phase 1).
2. For each *other* domain's `premises.md`, scan the `Depends on:`
   lines. Whenever a depends-on points back at a touched domain,
   open both premises and verify the diff still honors the
   dependency.
3. For any new or modified premise (file-level), check that any
   premise in other domains that should now `Depends on:` it is
   listed. Missing dependencies in `Depends on:` are *also* findings
   — they accumulate silently and break the cross-domain agent on
   future PRs.
4. Cross-reference contracts: if the diff changes `CollisionMessage`,
   `EntitySpawnRequest`, `LoadLevelRequest`, or any other public
   message, walk every consumer and confirm it handles the new
   shape.

### Agent 5 — Premises / Test-Coverage (Opus, eco-swappable to Sonnet)

**Persona.** You are the engineer who maps every premise in
`docs/{domain}/premises.md` to a test in `MonoDreams.Tests/`. You
flag two things: premises with `Tests: none yet` that the diff
makes urgent, and brand-new premises the diff introduces that the
docs don't yet name.

**Embedded tenets.** CORE_TENETS §2 — "Public contracts must be
backed by a test or example that exercises them." Every premises
file's "Follow-up debt" section.

**Checklist.**
1. For each premises file relevant to the diff (per Phase 1
   routing):
   - List the premises with `Tests: none yet`.
   - For each, ask: does the diff exercise this premise's path? If
     yes, and the diff didn't add a test, **Medium** finding:
     "premise X is now exercised by new code but still has
     `Tests: none yet`; consider adding a test in this PR."
2. Walk the diff for **new premises the docs don't yet name.** A new
   component, system, message, or invariant introduced by the PR is
   itself a new premise the docs should record. Examples:
   - New tag component → who manages it? Premise.
   - New message type → who emits, who consumes? Premise.
   - New system that depends on another running first → ordering
     premise.
   - For each, propose the premise text (one paragraph + Why /
     Breaks / Tests / Depends on).
3. If the diff adds a new public message, component, or system
   without a test or example, **High** finding:
   "Public contract added without a test/example that exercises it.
   CORE_TENETS §2 requires every contract to be maintained — without
   a use site it is indistinguishable from dead code."

### Agent 6 — ECS-Purity (Opus, eco-swappable to Sonnet)

**Persona.** You are the engineer who enforces the architectural
discipline. Components are pure data; systems are pure functions;
ordering belongs to the assembler. You flag any drift: logic creeping
into components, parallel renderers, shadowed namespaces, systems
that read state nobody told them about.

**Embedded tenets.** CORE_TENETS §2 — ECS purity & composition.

**Checklist.**
1. **Component purity.** Any new or modified `MonoDreams/Component/**`
   or `MonoDreams.Examples/Component/**` file: check that every
   member is a field or a trivial property. Methods that do logic →
   finding.
2. **System purity / pure-function shape.** A system that internally
   assumes another system ran first (without that being arranged by
   the screen) → finding. Watch for `Logger.Warning("X did not run
   yet")` patterns, or fallbacks that paper over ordering bugs.
3. **No parallel renderers.** Anything that calls `SpriteBatch.Draw`,
   `SpriteBatch.Begin`, etc. outside `MasterRenderSystem` → Blocker.
4. **No parallel level loading paths.** Anything that adds
   `CurrentLevelComponent` outside `LevelLoadRequestSystem` (excluding
   tests/tools that legitimately use the component-driven trigger
   pattern) → High.
5. **Namespace integrity.** Anything placed under `MonoDreams.Entity`
   → Blocker (shadows `DefaultEcs.Entity`). Anything placed under
   `MonoDreams.Camera` namespace conflicting with the `Camera` class
   → High.
6. **`Visible` ownership.** Game code that adds or removes `Visible`
   outside `CullingSystem` → High (see Rendering premises).
7. **`ColliderTag` ownership.** Manual adds/removes outside the
   auto-apply machinery → High.

---

## Phase 3 — Consolidate

Receive all six agent reports. Then:

1. **Dedupe.** Multiple agents will catch the same bug from
   different angles. Keep the most specific framing; cite which
   lenses caught it.
2. **Verify every Blocker and High.** For each, read the actual file
   at the cited path and confirm the code matches what the agent
   described. **Never dismiss a finding because the local file
   "looks different" — that means you may be on the wrong branch.
   Recheck Phase 0 first.** If the file genuinely doesn't say what
   the agent claimed, demote or drop the finding, and note the
   agent hallucinated.
3. **Classify.**
   - **Blocker** — framework-violating, will silently corrupt
     gameplay or the engine model (parallel renderer, namespace
     shadowing, missed enum case in critical filter).
   - **High** — premise violation, missing test for newly-exercised
     premise, framework-fit problem on a public primitive, missed
     downstream caller.
   - **Medium** — convention deviation, missing test for premise
     that *might* be exercised, opportunity to extend an existing
     primitive instead of adding a new one.
   - **Low** — naming nits, doc updates, refactor opportunities,
     premise-text suggestions.

---

## Phase 4 — Present and route

Render the consolidated review as a single markdown block:

```
# Deep review of <PR #N | branch <name> | commit <sha> | local changes>

**Mode:** <pr/branch/commit/local>
**Base:** <origin/main or <sha>~1>
**Files changed:** <count>
**Lenses applied:** <list of 6 agents>

## Blockers
<findings or "None.">

## High
<findings>

## Medium
<findings>

## Low
<findings>

## New premises proposed
<from Agent 5 — premise-text drafts that the docs should record after the PR lands>

## Premises now urgent
<from Agent 5 — `Tests: none yet` items the PR exercises>
```

Then ask the user where to send it via `AskUserQuestion`:

- *(PR mode only)* **Post to GitHub** — `gh pr review <n> --comment
  --body-file <tempfile>`. Confirm with the user before posting; the
  comment is visible publicly.
- **Copy to clipboard** — `pbcopy < <tempfile>` on macOS.
- **Save to file** — at a path the user picks, default
  `./deep-review-<timestamp>.md`.
- **Nothing** — keep the review in chat only.

If the user declines any action, the review still exists in the chat
transcript for their reference.

---

## Operational notes

- **Don't be cautious for the sake of it.** A "Low" finding that
  says "consider naming this differently" is noise unless the name
  actively misleads. Agents should return `No findings.` more often
  than they probably will at first; iterate the prompts above if
  Low-finding inflation becomes a problem.
- **Hallucinated paths are the #1 failure mode of Phase 2.** That's
  why Phase 3 re-verifies every Blocker/High. Trust the file on
  disk, not the agent's recollection.
- **The skill is calibrated for MonoDreams.** It cites tenets,
  premises, and anchors specific to this engine. Do not run it in
  another repo without re-tuning the agent personas and anchors.
- **Premises evolve.** When Phase 4 surfaces new premises Agent 5
  proposed, encourage the user to fold them into the relevant
  `docs/<domain>/premises.md` after merging. The skill's value
  compounds with the docs.

1	# About this project
2	This project is a code-first and ECS-purist 2D game engine built on MonoGame
3	(rendering) and DefaultEcs (ECS framework). The core concept is plug'n play
4	components and systems: add a `Transform` and `RigidBody` to an entity, include
5	`GravitySystem` in your pipeline, and gravity just works.
6	
7	MonoDreams is still in alpha. The core library (`MonoDreams/`) is the
8	authoritative source for all engine infrastructure — rendering, camera, cursor,
9	collision, physics, entity spawning, level loading, and screen management.
10	`MonoDreams.Examples/` contains game-specdific logic only. Your starting point to
11	understand how to wire up a game screen is
12	`MonoDreams.Examples/Screens/LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs`.
13	
14	# Project structure
15	- `MonoDreams/` — core engine library: components, systems, rendering, camera,
16	  cursor, collision, physics, entity spawning, level loading, screen management
17	- `MonoDreams.Examples/` — game-specific logic: screens, input mapping,
18	  dialogue, movement, entity factories, settings
19	- `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` — YarnSpinner dialogue integration (standalone, not
20	  referenced by core)
21	- `MonoDreams.Tests/` — tests
22	- `Tools/` — Blender exporter plugin for level design
23	
24	# Key conventions
25	
26	## Component design
27	- Components are pure data containers — no logic, no methods beyond simple
28	  helpers. All behavior lives in systems.
29	- Before creating a new component, check if an existing one can be extended
30	  with a field or flag. This project avoids component sprawl.
31	- `EntityInfo` is string-based in core (`new EntityInfo("Player")`). Game code
32	  can define its own enum for convenience.
33	- `Transform` is the single spatial component — there is no separate Position
34	  component.
35	- `CameraFollowTarget` lives in `MonoDreams.Component` (not a Camera
36	  subdirectory) to avoid namespace conflicts with the `Camera` class.
37	- `DrawComponent` (class) is the unified rendering component — it supports
38	  Sprite, Text, NinePatch, and Mesh via the `DrawElementType` enum. **Do not
39	  create new draw/render components.**
40	- `SpriteInfo` (struct) holds sprite source data (texture, source rect, color,
41	  layer depth). Both `SpriteInfo` and `DrawComponent` are set on entities that
42	  render.
43	- `Visible` is an empty tag struct added/removed by `CullingSystem`. Entities
44	  need it to be rendered.
45	
46	## Entity creation
47	- Factory-based: implement `IEntityFactory` (in `MonoDreams.EntityFactory`),
48	  register it with `EntitySpawnSystem` (in `MonoDreams.System.EntitySpawn`) by
49	  string identifier. The system listens for `EntitySpawnRequest` messages and
50	  dispatches to the right factory.
51	- Namespace choice: `MonoDreams.EntityFactory` (not `.Entity`) to avoid
52	  shadowing `DefaultEcs.Entity`.
53	- Direct creation: `BlenderLevelParserSystem` creates entities from exported
54	  Blender level data.
55	- Standard component stack for a renderable entity: `EntityInfo`, `Transform`,
56	  physics components as needed, `SpriteInfo`, `DrawComponent`, `Visible`.
57	
58	## Rendering pipeline
59	- All rendering infrastructure lives in `MonoDreams.Component.Draw` and
60	  `MonoDreams.System.Draw`.
61	- Three render targets defined by `RenderTargetID`: Main (game world, camera
62	  transform applied), UI, HUD.
63	- Draw pipeline: prep systems (`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`,
64	  `MeshPrepSystem`) populate `DrawComponent` from source data →
65	  `MasterRenderSystem` renders everything.
66	- `MasterRenderSystem` is game-agnostic and handles all draw types. Do not
67	  create parallel render systems.
68	- `CullingSystem` adds/removes the `Visible` component based on camera view
69	  bounds.
70	
71	## Collision and physics
72	- `BoxCollider`, `RigidBody`, `Velocity` components in
73	  `MonoDreams.Component.Collision` / `MonoDreams.Component.Physics`.
74	- Transform-based collision detection and resolution in
75	  `MonoDreams.System.Collision`.
76	- `GravitySystem` in `MonoDreams.System.Physics`.
77	
78	## Level loading
79	- LDtk and Blender parsers in `MonoDreams.System.Level`.
80	- `LoadLevelRequest` message triggers the pipeline.
81	- `LevelLoadRequestSystem` → parser systems → `EntitySpawnSystem`.
82	
83	## Debug infrastructure
84	- **Logger** — `MonoDreams.State.Logger`, replaces `Console.WriteLine`. Writes
85	  to `debug/monodreams_*.log` with `[wallclock] [GT gametime] [LEVEL] message`
86	  format. Call `Logger.Info(msg)`, `.Debug()`, `.Warning()`, `.Error()`.
87	- **Input replay** — place `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output dir.
88	  Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type, time }] }`.
89	  `startLevel` skips menus and jumps straight to the game screen. Actions match
90	  `AInputState` names (Up, Down, Left, Right, Jump, Grab, Orb, Exit, Interact).
91	  Game auto-exits when replay finishes.
92	- **Screenshots** — `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` saves PNGs every 2s to `debug/`.
93	  Off by default; enable by setting `"screenshots": true` in `input_replay.json`.
94	- **Running a test session** — write `input_replay.json`, run
95	  `dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples`, check `debug/` for log +
96	  screenshots.
97	- **Headless mode** — `dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`
98	  skips rendering, runs at max speed (no VSync, no fixed timestep), for
99	  automated testing. The game window is created at 1×1 off-screen.
100	- **Debug directory override** — set `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR` env var to redirect
101	  all debug output (logs, replay input, screenshots) to a custom path. Used by
102	  the test runner for parallel test isolation.
103	
104	## Testing
105	- Run tests: `dotnet test MonoDreams.Tests/`
106	- Integration tests use headless replay + log assertions via `GameTestRunner`.
107	- `GameTestRunner` spawns the game in headless mode with a temp debug dir,
108	  writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and provides log assertion
109	  helpers (`AssertLogContains`, `AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`).
110	
111	# Workflow
112	
113	**Before any non-trivial implementation, read the docs.** The
114	`docs/` layer (see the Documentation section below) captures engine
115	invariants that are silently load-bearing — most "surprising" bugs in
116	this repo come from violating one of them. Skipping this step is the

119	
120	1. **Always** read [`docs/CORE_TENETS.md`](../docs/CORE_TENETS.md)
121	   before any task that adds, removes, or significantly modifies a
122	   component, system, message, screen, or factory.

1	# MonoDreams — Core Tenets
2	
3	> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
4	> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
5	> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
6	> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.
7	
8	## 1. Framework, not library
9	
10	MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
11	the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
12	the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
13	embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
14	low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
15	(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).
16	
17	**Two users, equal weight.**
18	- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
19	  play primitives.
20	- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
21	  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
22	  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.
23	
24	**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
25	general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
26	than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
27	hiding inside the framework.
28	
29	## 2. ECS purity & composition
30	
31	The architecture is composition all the way down:
32	
33	- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
34	  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
35	  logic belongs in a system.
36	- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
37	  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
38	  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
39	  run after.
40	- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
41	  their own.
42	- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
43	  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
44	  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
45	  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
46	  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.
47	
48	**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
49	more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
50	are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
51	should always have more systems than components.
52	
53	**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
54	search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
55	creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
56	this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
57	of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
58	reusable.
59	
60	**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
61	systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
62	Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
63	dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
64	name alone.
65	
66	**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
67	system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
68	just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
69	generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
70	isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.
71	
72	### Aspirational direction
73	
74	- **Declarative system dependencies.** Today, ordering is implicit in
75	  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
76	  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
77	  enforce or warn at registration time.
78	- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
79	  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
80	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
81	  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
82	  closest prototype.
83	- **Test or example per public contract.** New messages, components, and
84	  systems should ship with at least one usage that proves the contract
85	  works and signals that it's maintained.
86	
87	## 3. Hierarchy & Transform
88	
89	`Transform` is the engine's spatial component today. It holds position,
90	rotation, scale, origin, and an optional parent link; it caches a world
91	matrix and exposes `WorldPosition` / `WorldRotation` / `WorldScale`
92	properties that walk the parent chain.
93	
94	**Key invariant — don't mix two Transform-shaped components in one
95	project.** A developer is free to write a `MyTransform` with different
96	trade-offs; what breaks the framework is **mixing** `Transform` and
97	`MyTransform` in the same world. Systems should be agnostic enough to
98	operate on either one (see §2 — systems are functions), but the bundled
99	collision, rendering, camera, and culling systems read `Transform`
100	specifically. Using a custom transform means re-implementing those
101	consumers too.
102	
103	**Two parent links, intentionally.** `Transform.Parent` is the matrix
104	link (it determines how `WorldMatrix` cascades); `ChildOf` is a
105	structural marker (it determines lifecycle and cascading disposal). The
106	split exists to support complex hierarchical UI such as a dialogue
107	panel — a single visual whose banner, avatars, text and waiting-indicator
108	move and dispose together but may not all share matrix scaling.
109	`HierarchySystem` keeps the two in sync. **This split is on the refactor
110	backlog** (§9); read both fields when reasoning about hierarchy until it
111	is consolidated.
112	
113	**Dirty propagation.** Mutating a parent's transform marks the entire
114	descendant chain dirty; `WorldMatrix` is a cached property whose getter
115	re-walks the chain when needed. Systems that read `WorldPosition` get
116	the parent-corrected value, but only if `HierarchySystem` has run in the
117	pipeline ahead of them — that's the pipeline assembler's job to arrange.
118	
119	**`Transform.Delta` and `HasMoved`.** These reflect the change between
120	two committed positions. They are meaningful only after
121	`TransformCommitSystem` has run for the *previous* frame. Today no API
122	prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; this is on the backlog as
123	"`Transform` should expose interaction methods that guarantee `Delta`
124	consistency" (§9). For now, downstream systems that depend on `Delta`
125	(notably the collision detection's swept tests) must trust the
126	assembler put `TransformCommitSystem` at the end of every frame.
127	
128	### Aspirational direction
129	
130	Collision, rendering, culling, and camera all read `Transform`
131	directly. The intended end-state is loose coupling — those modules
132	operate against any *Transform-shaped contract*, so a developer can
133	swap in `MyTransform` without re-implementing them. The framework
134	currently doesn't enforce this; treat any `MonoDreams/System/`
135	reference to `Transform` as implementation debt rather than design.

137	## 4. Rendering pipeline
138	
139	The rendering pipeline is the most delicate part of the engine. Bugs
140	here are visual rather than logical, which makes them harder to debug
141	than crashes. Two rules cover most of the surface:
142	
143	**Key invariant — `DrawComponent` is the unified render component.**
144	There is one `DrawComponent` per renderable entity. Its `Type` field is
145	one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, mutually exclusive.
146	Source data lives in companion structs (`SpriteInfo`, `DynamicText`,
147	`NinePatchInfo`, mesh buffers) populated by prep systems
148	(`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, `MeshPrepSystem`).
149	**Do not create new draw/render components.** Adding a new visual type
150	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork
151	the pipeline.
152	
153	**Key invariant — `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer.** No game
154	code should call `SpriteBatch` outside the prep-then-master path. A
155	parallel render system is a framework violation — flagged by review.
156	
157	**Key rule — rendering systems run last.** In any pipeline assembly,
158	the prep-cull-sort-render block goes at the end. The recommended order
159	inside the block, from the reference assembly
160	(`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331`), is:
161	`CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` → `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem`
162	→ `MeshPrepSystem` → `MasterRenderSystem`.
163	
164	**Render targets.** Three are defined by `RenderTargetID`:
165	- **Main** — world-space, camera transform applied, **respects culling**.
166	- **UI** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
167	- **HUD** — screen-space, no camera transform, always renders.
168

170	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. Only the Main target consults it. UI and

173	outcome anyway — but the failure mode is the reverse: a Main-target
174	entity that never gets `Visible` because no `CullingSystem` is in the

176	entity stack is therefore `EntityInfo + Transform + SpriteInfo +
177	DrawComponent + Visible` for Main, minus `Visible` for UI/HUD.

179	`DrawComponent` to remove the easy-to-miss tag.
180	
181	**Layer depth ownership.** Three systems write `LayerDepth`, in this
182	order: `SpritePrepSystem` initializes it from the sprite's layer,
183	`YSortSystem` may override it for entities on Y-sorted layers, and
184	`MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final value. `YSortSystem` uses a
185	minimal epsilon to bias parent-child groups so children stay attached
186	to their parent's depth band. Same-layer entities with the same world Y
187	fall through to insertion order — no other tiebreaker exists; if
188	flicker becomes a problem, that's where to look.
189	
190	**Camera.** A `Camera` instance owns its virtual resolution
191	(immutable after construction) and exposes mutable zoom, position, and
192	rotation. Multiple cameras at once are explicitly supported — local
193	multiplayer or CCTV-style views. `CameraFollowSystem` is *optional*:
194	fixed-camera games or custom camera systems are valid; just don't
195	register `CameraFollowSystem` and `CullingSystem` will still read
196	whatever the `Camera` reports.

198	## 5. Physics & collision
199	
200	The framework provides Newtonian-style movement, gravity, layer-based
201	collision filtering, and AABB plus convex-polygon (SAT) collision
202	detection. These pieces are independent components and systems — a
203	game can use velocity without collision, or collision without
204	gravity — and the pipeline assembler picks which to register.
205	
206	**Components.** `Velocity` carries current and last velocity vectors
207	(the delta is exposed); `RigidBody` carries mass, gravity participation,
208	kinematic flag, and freeze-axis flags; `BoxCollider` carries an AABB
209	and active layers; `ConvexCollider` carries model-space vertices,
210	world-space vertices, a broadphase AABB and active layers. `ColliderTag`
211	is auto-applied to any entity with a collider component so detection
212	queries can match a unified tag.
213	
214	**The reference physics pipeline order**, from
215	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–286`:
216	**Movement → Velocity → Detection → Resolution → Commit.**
217	Each stage owns one job:
218	- *Movement* — game systems write `Velocity` based on input and AI.
219	- *Velocity (`VelocitySystem`)* — apply `Velocity` to `Transform.Position`.
220	- *Detection (`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`)* — broadphase via AABB
221	  + narrowphase via SAT for `ConvexCollider`; emit `CollisionMessage`s.
222	- *Resolution (`TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` or
223	  `TransformPhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`)* — correct positions and
224	  velocities for contacts; honor `RigidBody` freeze flags.
225	- *Commit (`TransformCommitSystem`)* — finalize `LastPosition`, so the
226	  next frame's `Delta` is meaningful.
227	
228	Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
229	reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
230	ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
231	through walls — see §3.
232	
233	**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
234	the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
235	filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
236	broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
237	that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
238	broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.
239	
240	**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
241	holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
242	thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
243	contexts.
244	
245	**One collider of each type per entity.** Today the framework assumes
246	an entity has at most one `BoxCollider` and at most one `ConvexCollider`.
247	This is implicit, not enforced. Multiple colliders of the same type on
248	a single entity is undefined behavior — if you need it, that's a
249	framework change, not a workaround.
250	
251	### Aspirational direction
252	
253	Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
254	end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.
255	
256	## 6. Level loading & entity spawning
257	
258	Levels live in `.ldtk` files (LDtk editor) and `.json` exports from
259	Blender (`Tools/blender_level_export.py`). The pipeline is identical
260	in shape: a request loads a file, a parser walks the data, and the
261	parser emits `EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into
262	entities.
263	
264	**The pipeline.**
265	1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
266	2. `LevelLoadRequestSystem` consumes the request, loads the file, and
267	   **adds `CurrentLevelComponent` to the world**. The background colour
268	   lands as `CurrentBackgroundColorComponent`.
269	3. Parser systems (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`,
270	   `BlenderLevelParserSystem`) **subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
271	   being added** — not to the message. They parse on add and emit
272	   `EntitySpawnRequest`s.
273	4. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
274	   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.
275	
276	**Key invariant — systems react to component lifecycle, not to push
277	messages.** The parser pattern (subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
278	added) is the engine-wide default. A test or tool that adds
279	`CurrentLevelComponent` manually triggers the parsers just as well as
280	the regular `LoadLevelRequest` path. Resist the urge to make a system

282	system to an upstream sequence that should be the assembler's choice.
283

285	`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
286	setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
287	warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
288	throw** — this is on the backlog (§9). For now, treat the warning as a
289	high-severity signal during development.
290

292	identifier; if it starts with `Blender_`, the Blender parser handles
293	it, otherwise the LDtk parser does. **This dispatch by name prefix is
294	a quick hack** (§9); a content-driven dispatch (a format field in the
295	level data) is the eventual replacement.

298	
299	`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
300	assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
301	overall order, end-to-end:
302	
303	1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
304	   under replay.
305	2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
306	   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
307	   dialogue state).
308	3. **Physics block** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
309	   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
310	   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
311	   `TransformCommitSystem`.
312	4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
313	   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
314	5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
315	6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
316	7. **Render block** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →

334	tests.

339	*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.

351	time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
352	skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
353	auto-exits when the replay finishes.
354	
355	**Screenshots.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` saves PNGs every 2 seconds to

358

380	field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.

388	
389	- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
390	  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
391	  reasoning about hierarchy.
392	- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
393	  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
394	  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
395	- **`Blender_` identifier prefix** (§6). Dispatch by name prefix is a
396	  hack; a content-driven dispatch (format field in level data) is the
397	  eventual replacement.
398	- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
399	  Intended behaviour is to throw.
400	- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
401	  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
402	  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
403	- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
404	  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
405	  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
406	  contract.

410	  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
411	- **Headless mode is experimental** (§8). Original intent was AI-agent
412	  visual testing; current implementation is not stable enough to be
413	  load-bearing.
414	- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
415	  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today.
416	- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
417	  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
418	  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.

421	  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
422	  contract should ship with at least one usage.

# MonoDreams — Core Tenets

> The invariants and design principles that hold across the engine.
> Read this before working on MonoDreams — most of what looks surprising in
> the code is consistent with one of these tenets. AI coding agents should
> load this file as context for any non-trivial task in the repo.

## 1. Framework, not library

MonoDreams is to game devs what Spring is to web devs: the framework owns
the heavy lifting (rendering, camera, physics, level loading, spawning),
the developer owns the gameplay code, and the price of full control is
embracing ECS. The competitive position is between **bare MonoGame** (too
low-level — you write the rendering loop yourself) and **Nez or similar**
(too loose — you give up control to get convenience).

**Two users, equal weight.**
- Solo devs and small indie teams who *like writing code* and want plug'n
  play primitives.
- AI coding agents (Claude Code and similar) operating on the codebase.
  Docs in this repo — CORE_TENETS, premises files, CLAUDE.md — are
  first-class context for that user, not human-only supplementary material.

**Key rule.** When choosing between a more specialized API and a more
general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more
than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction
hiding inside the framework.

## 2. ECS purity & composition

The architecture is composition all the way down:

- **Components** are pure data containers. No logic, no methods beyond
  trivial property getters. If you reach for a method on a component, the
  logic belongs in a system.
- **Systems** are pure functions over components. A system declares the
  components it operates on and acts on every entity that matches. It
  makes **no assumption** about which other systems ran before or will
  run after.
- **Entities** are IDs that group components. They carry no state of
  their own.
- **The pipeline assembler — the screen — owns ordering.** The screen
  registers systems in the order they should run for that screen's
  intended behavior. A system that quietly depends on another system
  having run is a framework-level bug; the dependency belongs in the
  pipeline assembly, not inside the system.

**Atomic unit of composition.** A new feature usually lands as one or
more new systems, sometimes paired with one new component. Components
are added only when there is genuinely new data to model. Net: the engine
should always have more systems than components.

**Discover before creating.** Before adding a component or system,
search what's already there. Prefer extending an existing component to
creating a new one (CLAUDE.md says the same — it is repeated here because
this is the most common review finding). The failure mode is a plethora
of micro-components, each solving one feature's narrow pain, none
reusable.

**Key invariant.** Public contracts — messages, components, public
systems — must be backed by a test or example that exercises them.
Contracts without a maintained use site become indistinguishable from
dead code, and the framework cannot signal "this is part of the API" by
name alone.

**Key rule (the #1 review lens).** When a PR adds a new component or
system, ask: *does this evolve well as more features land, or did we
just solve today's pain?* A hyper-specialized addition that doesn't
generalize is the framework's primary failure mode. If a generalization
isn't obvious, propose extending an existing primitive instead.

  the screen's registration order. A future API would let a system
  declare "I expect X to have run this frame" and let the framework
  enforce or warn at registration time.
- **Modular packs.** Today the engine is one bundle. The intended
  end-state is Spring-style modules (`MonoDreams.Rendering`,
  `MonoDreams.Physics`, `MonoDreams.Dialogue`, …) that can be adopted
  independently. The current `MonoDreams.YarnSpinner/` is the
  closest prototype.

Swept collision (the dynamic AABB-vs-AABB and convex-vs-convex tests)
reads `Transform.Delta`. Delta is correct only if the previous frame
ended with `TransformCommitSystem`. Skip `Commit` and collisions go
through walls — see §3.

**`ConvexCollider.BroadPhaseAABB`.** This AABB must be refreshed when
the world vertices change (transform moved or rotated). Detection
filters on it; a stale AABB makes a real collision invisible to the
broadphase. The detection system updates it; if you write a system
that mutates a convex collider's vertices directly, refresh the
broadphase AABB before the next detection pass.

**Single-threaded detection.** `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem`
holds instance-level polygon buffers. It is intentionally not
thread-safe; do not register two instances or invoke it from parallel
contexts.

**One collider of each type per entity.** Today the framework assumes
an entity has at most one `BoxCollider` and at most one `ConvexCollider`.
This is implicit, not enforced. Multiple colliders of the same type on
a single entity is undefined behavior — if you need it, that's a
framework change, not a workaround.

### Aspirational direction

Collision is currently coupled to `Transform` (see §3). The intended
end-state is collision against any Transform-shaped contract.

## 6. Level loading & entity spawning

Levels live in `.ldtk` files (LDtk editor) and `.json` exports from
Blender (`Tools/blender_level_export.py`). The pipeline is identical
in shape: a request loads a file, a parser walks the data, and the
parser emits `EntitySpawnRequest` messages that a factory turns into
entities.

**The pipeline.**
1. Game code publishes `LoadLevelRequest`.
2. `LevelLoadRequestSystem` consumes the request, loads the file, and
   **adds `CurrentLevelComponent` to the world**. The background colour
   lands as `CurrentBackgroundColorComponent`.
3. Parser systems (`LDtkEntityParserSystem`, `LDtkTileParserSystem`,
   `BlenderLevelParserSystem`) **subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
   being added** — not to the message. They parse on add and emit
   `EntitySpawnRequest`s.
4. `EntitySpawnSystem` consumes each spawn request and dispatches to an
   `IEntityFactory` registered for the request's string identifier.

**Key invariant — systems react to component lifecycle, not to push
messages.** The parser pattern (subscribe to `CurrentLevelComponent`
added) is the engine-wide default. A test or tool that adds
`CurrentLevelComponent` manually triggers the parsers just as well as
the regular `LoadLevelRequest` path. Resist the urge to make a system
"only respond when the right message arrived" — that's coupling the
system to an upstream sequence that should be the assembler's choice.

**Factory registration.** `EntitySpawnSystem` keeps a dictionary of
`string → IEntityFactory`. Game code registers factories at screen
setup time. Currently, an unregistered identifier produces a logged
warning and the spawn is silently dropped. **Intended behavior is to
throw** — this is on the backlog (§9). For now, treat the warning as a
high-severity signal during development.

**`Blender_` identifier prefix.** The level loader looks at the level
identifier; if it starts with `Blender_`, the Blender parser handles
it, otherwise the LDtk parser does. **This dispatch by name prefix is
a quick hack** (§9); a content-driven dispatch (a format field in the
level data) is the eventual replacement.

## 7. The reference pipeline

`LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:277–331` is the gold-standard pipeline
assembly. Read it before composing a new screen. The recommended
overall order, end-to-end:

1. **Input** — keyboard/mouse polling, `InputReplaySystem` if running
   under replay.
2. **Game logic** — game-specific systems that read input and entity
   state to update gameplay components (movement intent, AI decisions,
   dialogue state).
3. **Physics block** — `MovementSystem` → `VelocitySystem` →
   `TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` →
   `TransformCollisionResolutionSystem` (or `…PhysicalCollisionResolutionSystem`) →
   `TransformCommitSystem`.
4. **Hierarchy** — `HierarchySystem` (then `TransformCommitSystem` if
   children moved independently), `SizeSystem`, `LayoutSystem`.
5. **Camera** — `CameraFollowSystem` (optional).
6. **Cursor** — `CursorInputSystem`, `CursorPositionSystem`.
7. **Render block** — `CullingSystem` → `SpritePrepSystem` →
   `YSortSystem` → `TextPrepSystem` → `MeshPrepSystem` →
   `MasterRenderSystem` → debug overlays.

Each game's screen owns its own pipeline. The reference assembly is a
recommendation — fixed-camera games omit `CameraFollowSystem`,
non-physics screens skip the physics block, UI-only screens may have
no game logic at all. What does not change is the *shape* of the order:
input first, render last, with physics ahead of hierarchy and hierarchy
ahead of culling.

### Aspirational direction

A declarative system-dependencies API would let
`TransformCollisionDetectionSystem` say "I need `VelocitySystem` before
me this frame" and let the framework validate the assembly. Until that
exists, ordering bugs are caught by review (see the `/deep-review`
skill at §`.claude/skills/deep-review/SKILL.md`) and by behaviour
tests.

## 8. Debug & testing

The engine provides a small set of debug primitives. They are
*available*, not *required* — most screens register none of them.

**`Logger`.** A static, lock-protected singleton in
`MonoDreams.State.Logger`. `Initialize(outputDirectory)` must be called
once before use; `Shutdown()` must be called to flush. Output goes to
`<dir>/monodreams_<timestamp>.log` with format `[wallclock] [GT gametime]
[LEVEL] message`. Replaces `Console.WriteLine`. The `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR`
environment variable redirects all debug output (logs, replay input,
screenshots) for test isolation.

**Input replay.** Drop `debug/input_replay.json` in the build output
directory. Format: `{ startLevel, description, commands: [{ action, type,
time }] }`. Actions match `AInputState` names. The `startLevel` field
skips menus and jumps straight into the named game screen. The game
auto-exits when the replay finishes.

**Screenshots.** `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` saves PNGs every 2 seconds to
the debug directory. Off by default; enable by setting `"screenshots":
true` in `input_replay.json`.

**Headless mode.** `dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless`
creates a 1×1 off-screen window, disables VSync, removes the fixed
timestep, and runs at maximum speed. **This is experimental and not
load-bearing.** It is convenient for fast integration tests via
`GameTestRunner` and was originally intended to let AI agents
"visually" test gameplay, but the implementation is not currently
trusted as a stable testing contract — flakes and missing edge cases
should be expected. Tests that need rendering correctness should not
rely on it.

**Testing.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` uses xUnit + the custom
`GameTestRunner`, which spawns the game in headless mode with a temp
debug directory, writes an `InputReplayPlan`, waits for exit, and
exposes log-assertion helpers (`AssertLogContains`,
`AssertLogContainsInOrder`, `GetLogLines`). The gold-standard tests
today are `SATCollisionTests` (pure-logic), `BlenderLevelTests`
(parsing), and `InfiniteRunnerTests` (integration).

**No architectural tests today.** ArchUnit-style assertions
("`MonoDreams/Component/*.cs` must contain only data") do not exist
yet. Most premises in `docs/{domain}/premises.md` start their `Tests:`
field as `none yet`; introducing architectural tests is on the backlog.

## 9. Refactor backlog (named cruft)

Carried forward from the bootstrap interview so they are not forgotten.
Each is either implementation debt or an aspirational direction that
will eventually move from "documented in CORE_TENETS" to "enforced in
code".

- **`ChildOf` vs `Transform.Parent` split** (§3). Two parent links
  exist today; consolidation desired. Until then, read both when
  reasoning about hierarchy.
- **`Visible` as a tag** (§4). Could become `DrawComponent.Visible`.
  Open question: would moving it complicate the bulk add/remove
  pattern `CullingSystem` uses today?
- **`Blender_` identifier prefix** (§6). Dispatch by name prefix is a
  hack; a content-driven dispatch (format field in level data) is the
  eventual replacement.
- **`EntitySpawnSystem` silent-drops unregistered factories** (§6).
  Intended behaviour is to throw.
- **`Transform.Delta` consistency not enforced** (§3). No API today
  prevents reading stale `Delta` mid-frame; `Transform` should expose
  interaction methods that guarantee consistency.
- **Module-level coupling to `Transform`** (§3, §5). Collision,
  rendering, camera, culling all read `Transform` directly. The
  eventual end-state is loose coupling to any Transform-shaped
  contract.
- **Folder layout** (`Component/<subdomain>/` vs `Component/<file>/`
  inconsistency). Intended end-state is **modular packs** (Spring Data
  / Spring Security analog) — `MonoDreams.Rendering`,
  `MonoDreams.Physics`, etc. — that can be adopted independently.
- **Headless mode is experimental** (§8). Original intent was AI-agent
  visual testing; current implementation is not stable enough to be
  load-bearing.
- **No architectural tests** (§8). Most premises lack programmatic
  protection; review and discipline are the only enforcement today.
- **Declarative system dependencies** (§2, §7). A future API would let
  a system declare "I expect X to have run this frame" at registration
  time, replacing implicit-order discipline with explicit assertions.
- **Test or example per public contract** (§2). Several messages
  (`PositionChangeMessage`, `SizeChangeMessage`, `RigidBodyTouchMessage`)
  are exposed but may be leftovers without active consumers. Every
  contract should ship with at least one usage.

Why it's a problem: CORE_TENETS §1 — "When choosing between a more specialized API and a more general one, pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction." Today, every game system that wants edge detection has to invent its own bookkeeping field, get the ordering right (read `Pressed` *before* writing back to `XxxHeld`), and remember to seed the initial value (the PR has to set `InteractHeld = true` on `StartYarnDialogue` precisely because the auto-open keeps the press level-high for one more frame — every future edge-detecting system will hit this same trap).

Suggested fix: Not a blocker for this PR — it solves today's bug correctly. # Deep review of PR #23 — "Fix dialogue UI text overlap and option key-repeat"

**Mode:** PR
**Base:** merge-base `a146fd8` (PR #22 merge). `origin/main` has one additional `docs` commit on top.
**Files changed:** 3 (`MonoDreams.Examples/Component/Dialogue/DialogueState.cs`, `MonoDreams.Examples/System/Dialogue/DialogueSystem.cs`, `MonoDreams/System/Draw/TextPrepSystem.cs`)
**Lenses applied:** Adjacent-Code, System-Ordering, Component-Design/Framework-Fit, Cross-Domain Dependency, Premises/Test-Coverage, ECS-Purity

The PR cleanly fixes two real bugs (stale dialogue glyphs and option-row auto-repeat) and the behaviour is correct. The findings below cluster around a single core change — `TextPrepSystem`'s new "clear `DrawComponent.Text` on empty" branch — and around the per-system manual edge-detection pattern this PR doubles down on.

## Blockers
None.

## High

**[High] — `TextPrepSystem` empty-input branch is asymmetric, undocumented, and untested**
File: `MonoDreams/System/Draw/TextPrepSystem.cs:30-38`
What: When `DynamicText.VisibleCharacterCount <= 0` or text is empty, the new code mutates `existing.Text = null` on the entity's `DrawComponent`. The non-empty branch (line 47) instead calls `entity.Set(new DrawComponent { ... })` — a full replacement. This single change ships **five** issues that the review lenses caught in different ways:
1. **Partial clear vs. full replace.** Empty path zeroes only `Text`; non-empty path replaces every field. A future renderer change (e.g. rendering a placeholder for `Font != null && Text == null`) would unmask the stale `Font`/`Position`/`Color`/`LayerDepth` left behind. `MasterRenderSystem.DrawElement` (`MonoDreams/System/Draw/MasterRenderSystem.cs:198-199`) currently saves us via `if (element.Font == null || element.Text == null) return;` — load-bearing, undocumented.
2. **Cross-system asymmetry.** `SpritePrepSystem` (`MonoDreams/System/Draw/SpritePrepSystem.cs:14`) declares `[With(..., typeof(Visible))]` and skips entirely when source is empty (no clear). `TextPrepSystem` skips `Visible` and now mutates on empty input. Two prep systems in the same block, two different contracts.
3. **Filter understates the system's interest set.** `[With(typeof(DynamicText), typeof(Transform))]` does not declare `DrawComponent`, hence the new `if (entity.Has<DrawComponent>())` guard. CORE_TENETS §2 ("A system declares the components it operates on") — the declared filter should match the real interest.
4. **No premise in `docs/rendering/premises.md`** documents the new "prep systems clear on empty" invariant. Future contributors maintaining `SpritePrepSystem` / `MeshPrepSystem` have no signpost that this contract exists. CLAUDE.md "Workflow when modifying a domain" mandates documenting new invariants in the same PR.
5. **No test.** `MonoDreams.Tests/` has zero coverage for `TextPrepSystem`, `DynamicText`, or text rendering. The very bug class this PR fixes (silent stale glyphs) is the one where a regression would be invisible until shipped. CORE_TENETS §2: "Public contracts must be backed by a test or example that exercises them."

Why it's a problem: each piece alone is small; together they're the canonical "framework-fit problem on a public primitive." The fix is correct *for the dialogue case the author tested* but the contract is fragile in ways future maintainers will trip on.

Suggested fix (in preference order):
- **(a) Implement the `ClearDrawComponentSystem` the reference screen already calls for.** `LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:321` has the literal comment `// new ClearDrawComponentSystem(_world),` at the head of the prep block. A single system that resets every `DrawComponent` to a known-blank shape every frame, with prep systems thereafter only writing fields when they have source, generalizes the "clear on empty" contract to all prep systems and lets `DialogueSystem.DeactivateDialogue` stop manually nulling `DrawComponent.Text`/`Font` (see Medium finding below).
- **(b) If (a) is too disruptive for this PR**, make the empty branch symmetric — replace the whole component (`entity.Set(new DrawComponent { Type = DrawElementType.Text, Target = text.Target })`) instead of half-clearing. Also: add `DrawComponent` to the `[With]` filter (so the guard goes away), fix the stale "(from base)" comment on line 12, add a unit test (pure-logic, ~30 lines: write empty `DynamicText`, run `TextPrepSystem`, assert `DrawComponent.Text == null`), and add a premise to `docs/rendering/premises.md` (draft text under "New premises proposed" below).

## Medium

**[Medium] — `StartYarnDialogue` sets `InteractHeld = true` unconditionally — wrong for the auto-trigger zone path**
File: `MonoDreams.Examples/System/Dialogue/DialogueSystem.cs:295`
What: Two paths call `StartYarnDialogue`:
- `OnDialogueStart` (line 261), published by `NPCInteractionSystem.cs:96` only when `InputState.Interact.Pressed(state)` — Interact *is* held, so `InteractHeld = true` is correct.
- `OnCollision` (line 270), fired on `CollisionType.Dialogue` from `GameCollisionHelper.cs:35` (`"Player" when targetType == "Zone"`) — the player walks into the zone without pressing Interact; `InteractHeld = true` is a lie.

Why it's a problem: the lie self-corrects within one frame (next `Update`: `interactNow = false`, then `_dialogueState.InteractHeld = interactNow = false`). Today no level in the example codebase actually tags an entity `"Zone"` (only `"NPCZone"`, see `LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs:220`), so the path is dormant. `DialogueZoneComponent` does carry an `autoStart` field, however, so the design intent included this path. Lighting up zones in a future level would surface a 1-frame loss of edge detection — small but a real contract mismatch.

Suggested fix: read the actual input state at the call site instead of asserting:
```csharp
_dialogueState.InteractHeld = InputState.Interact.Pressed(state); // needs GameState plumbed in
```
Or add a `bool consumeInteractPress` parameter and default it to `true` from `OnDialogueStart`, `false` from `OnCollision`. Long-term, the right fix is the framework primitive in the next finding — then this assumption disappears entirely.

**[Medium] — Per-system manual edge-detection is now in two places — missing framework primitive**
File: `MonoDreams.Examples/Component/Dialogue/DialogueState.cs:18-22`, `MonoDreams.Examples/System/Runner/RunnerMovementSystem.cs:36-43`
What: The diff comment is the smoking gun: *"Pressed() is level-triggered and engine JustPressed requires buffer > 0, so we track edges ourselves."* `RunnerMovementSystem` independently re-invents the same trick with `runnerState.JumpHeld`. `AInputState` (`MonoDreams/Input/AInputState.cs`) already owns `_pressed`, `_lastPressTime`, `_lastReleaseTime` — every ingredient to expose a frame-edge primitive is already there.

Why it's a problem: CORE_TENETS §1 — "Pick the general one. The same primitive should serve more than one feature; if it can't, it's probably a game-shaped abstraction hiding inside the framework." We now have N=2 game-code call sites paying per-key bookkeeping tax, with a third one (`LevelSelectionScreen` navigation, future menus) likely to repeat the pattern. Also accumulates input-subsystem state onto unrelated components (`DialogueState`, `RunnerState`).

Suggested fix: not a blocker for this PR — it solves today's bug correctly. But this PR should file the framework gap: add a backlog entry to `docs/CORE_TENETS.md` §9 ("Frame-edge input detection in `AInputState`") and a premise documenting the workaround idiom (draft under "New premises proposed" below). A follow-up PR can add `AInputState.WasPressedLastFrame` (snapshot at the end of `Update`) or a buffer-independent `JustPressedThisFrame(GameState)`. Once shipped, the three `XxxHeld` fields and `RunnerState.JumpHeld` go away.

**[Medium] — `DeactivateDialogue` duplicates work `TextPrepSystem` now owns**
File: `MonoDreams.Examples/System/Dialogue/DialogueSystem.cs:482-491`
What: With the new `TextPrepSystem` behaviour, lines 482-485 (`dynamicText.TextContent = ""; dynamicText.VisibleCharacterCount = 0;`) are sufficient — `TextPrepSystem` will null `DrawComponent.Text` next prep pass (same frame, since `DeactivateDialogue` runs inside the logic phase). The manual `textDraw.Text = null` (488) and `textDraw.Font = null` (489) are now redundant. The PR did not remove them.

Why it's a problem: duplicate responsibility creates uncertainty for future maintainers ("is this defensive or was it required?"). After the PR, the answer is "no longer required" — but the duplication remains. Same applies to the manual `boxDraw.Texture = null` (481) and `indicatorDraw.Texture = null` (495) lines — once a `ClearDrawComponentSystem` exists, all of these go.

Suggested fix: delete lines 480-481, 488-491, and 494-495 (the manual `*.Texture = null` / `textDraw.Text = null` / `textDraw.Font = null` cleanups). Verify with one playthrough that no flicker reappears. If keeping any for fast-path reasons, add a comment explaining why.

## Low

**[Low] — Stale `"(from base)"` comment on `TextPrepSystem` filter**
File: `MonoDreams/System/Draw/TextPrepSystem.cs:12`
What: The comment reads `// Ensures entities have these + DrawComponent (from base)`. There is no base filter that adds `DrawComponent` — `AEntitySetSystem<GameState>(world)` is the DefaultEcs base, no filter contribution. The new `if (entity.Has<DrawComponent>())` guard exists precisely because of the gap the comment papers over.
Suggested fix: replace with `// Ensures entities have these. DrawComponent is optional — created on demand below.` Or, if you take the High-finding fix and add `DrawComponent` to the `[With]`, just delete the dangling tail of the comment.

**[Low] — `Visible` on UI entities (pre-existing, not amplified)**
File: `MonoDreams.Examples/System/Dialogue/DialogueSystem.cs:300, 344-345, 428, 460-461, 477-478`
What: DialogueSystem manually adds/removes `Visible` on UI-target entities (BoxEntity, IndicatorEntity, OptionEntities). Per `docs/rendering/premises.md` "`Visible` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`", game code shouldn't touch `Visible` at all. Per "Three render targets, two behaviors", UI/HUD ignore `Visible` anyway, so the mutations are functionally no-ops today.
Why noted: not introduced or amplified by this PR — flagging only so the reviewer is aware. Out of scope to fix here.

## New premises proposed
*(Land these in `docs/rendering/premises.md` and `docs/CORE_TENETS.md` §9 alongside the PR, or in an immediate follow-up.)*

```
## Prep systems clear their slice of DrawComponent when input is empty

`SpritePrepSystem`, `TextPrepSystem`, and `MeshPrepSystem` each own one
slice of `DrawComponent` (sprite source, `Text`/`Font`, mesh buffers
respectively). When source data is empty or invalid for a frame
(`DynamicText.VisibleCharacterCount == 0`, empty mesh, missing sprite
source), the prep system must null/clear its slice on the existing
`DrawComponent`. Returning early without clearing leaves the previous
frame's data in place and `MasterRenderSystem` will render it again.

**Why:** `DrawComponent` is persistent across frames; prep systems are
the only writers for their slice. A prep system that goes quiet on an
entity whose `DrawComponent` has stale data leaves that data visible
indefinitely. This is the bug class fixed in PR #23.
**Breaks:** stale visuals (text from the previous Yarn line, sprites
from the previous frame, meshes from the previous state) silently
persist with no diagnostic.
**Tests:** none yet. Candidate: pure-logic test that writes empty
`DynamicText`, runs `TextPrepSystem`, asserts `DrawComponent.Text == null`.
**Depends on:** "`DrawComponent` is the only render component";
"`MasterRenderSystem` is the sole renderer".
```

```
## MasterRenderSystem skips DrawElements with null Text or null Font

`MasterRenderSystem.DrawElement` short-circuits on `element.Font == null ||
element.Text == null` for `DrawElementType.Text` (and the analogous
`element.Texture == null` for Sprite). This is the renderer-side half of
the "prep systems clear on empty" contract: a null sentinel field is the
prep system's signal that nothing should render this frame.

**Why:** clearing-as-null on the prep side and skip-on-null on the
renderer side must converge to "no draw call" for the pattern to work.
**Breaks:** removing the null guard (e.g. as paranoid defensive code in
a cleanup PR) silently regresses prep-side clearing.
**Tests:** none yet. Covered indirectly by the proposed TextPrepSystem
unit test.
**Depends on:** "Prep systems clear their slice of DrawComponent when
input is empty".
```

```
## Manual frame-edge input detection is the engine-wide idiom (for now)

`AInputState.Pressed(state)` is level-triggered. `AInputState.JustPressed`
requires a positive `buffer`; the default is 0, which makes it
effectively unusable for edge detection. Systems that need a
"key-just-pressed-this-frame" signal therefore track previous-frame held
state themselves: see `RunnerMovementSystem` (`JumpHeld`) and
`DialogueSystem` (`InteractHeld`, `UpHeld`, `DownHeld`).

**Why:** the engine has no frame-edge primitive today. Per-system
bookkeeping is the documented workaround until `AInputState` exposes an
edge trigger.
**Breaks:** systems that use `Pressed()` directly for "advance one step"
semantics auto-repeat at the framerate — the option-row bug fixed in
PR #23 is the canonical example.
**Tests:** none yet. Candidate: integration test that holds Interact for
N frames and asserts the dialogue advances exactly once.
**Depends on:** —
```

Also add to `docs/CORE_TENETS.md` §9 "Refactor backlog":
> - **Frame-edge input detection in `AInputState`.** `Pressed()` is
>   level-triggered; `JustPressed` needs `buffer > 0`. Game systems work
>   around this with per-key `XxxHeld` bookkeeping (see RunnerMovementSystem,
>   DialogueSystem). Future API: `WasPressedLastFrame` or a
>   buffer-independent `JustPressedThisFrame`.

## Premises now urgent

These have `Tests: none yet` in `docs/rendering/premises.md` and are *newly exercised* by PR 23 — landing the small unit test from the High finding above would cover them:

- **"Rendering systems run last in the pipeline"** — the PR's fix is correct only because `DialogueSystem` writes `DynamicText` before `TextPrepSystem` reads it. A future reorder would resurface the bug.
- The proposed new premise **"Prep systems clear their slice of `DrawComponent` when input is empty"** — would ship `Tests: <new test>` from day one.
